questions.title: Search algorithm
questions.text: A BST is stored in arrays `Left[]`, `Data[]`, `Right[]` with the variable `Root`; −1 means no child. Write an algorithm that searches for `Target` and outputs "Found" or "Not found".

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Current starts at Root (1)
- loop while Current <> −1 and Data[Current] <> Target (1)
- go Left if Target smaller else Right (1)
- output Found / Not found after the loop (1)
scheme.model_answer:
```pseudocode
Current ← Root
WHILE Current <> -1 AND Data[Current] <> Target DO
    IF Target < Data[Current] THEN
        Current ← Left[Current]
    ELSE
        Current ← Right[Current]
    ENDIF
ENDWHILE
IF Current = -1 THEN
    OUTPUT "Not found"
ELSE
    OUTPUT "Found"
ENDIF
```

- Every value goes to the right → the tree is a single chain / unbalanced (1)
- a search may visit every node (like a linear search) instead of about log₂ n (1)
scheme.model_answer: Each new value is larger, so it goes right every time and the tree becomes one long chain; searching for 50 needs 5 comparisons, as slow as a linear search.

questions.title: Searching
questions.text: A library stores book codes in a binary search tree held in arrays `Left[]`, `Data[]` and `Right[]`, with the variable `Root`.

parts.title: Algorithm
parts.text: Write an algorithm that searches the tree for `Code` and outputs "Found" or "Not found".

scheme.mark_scheme:
- start at Root (1)
- loop until −1 or found (1)
- compare and move Left / Right (1)
- correct output (1)
scheme.model_answer:
```pseudocode
Current ← Root
WHILE Current <> -1 AND Data[Current] <> Code DO
    IF Code < Data[Current] THEN
        Current ← Left[Current]
    ELSE
        Current ← Right[Current]
    ENDIF
ENDWHILE
IF Current = -1 THEN OUTPUT "Not found" ELSE OUTPUT "Found"
```

parts.title: Why BST
parts.text: Explain why searching a BST is usually faster than a linear search, and when it may not be.

scheme.mark_scheme: Each comparison discards half / a whole subtree (1); about log₂ n comparisons for a balanced tree vs up to n for linear (1); if data inserted in sorted order the tree is unbalanced / a chain, so up to n comparisons (1)
scheme.model_answer: At every node the search goes left or right, ignoring the other subtree, so a balanced tree needs about log₂ n comparisons rather than n. But if the codes were inserted in sorted order the tree is a chain and the search is as slow as a linear search.

summary: Tree terminology, binary trees and binary search trees, building a BST from numbers and strings, storing it as nodes with left pointer, data and right pointer, inserting and searching with a trace, in-order, pre-order and post-order traversals, balanced and unbalanced trees, and where binary trees are used.

blocks.content: A **hierarchical** (non-linear) data structure made of **nodes** joined by **branches (edges)**. It has one **root** at the top; every other node has exactly **one parent**.
A tree in which each node has **at most two children**: a **left** child and a **right** child.

blocks.title: Inserting a value
items: If the new value is **smaller** than the node, go **left**; if it is **greater (or equal)**, go **right**.
Repeat until you reach an **empty** position, and attach the new node there.
Values must be inserted **in the order given** — a different order gives a different tree.

blocks.content: The result is the tree drawn in the previous section.

blocks.title: A BST of strings: "M", "B", "A", "K", "H", "V", "T"
blocks.content:
```text
                 [M]
               /     \
            [B]       [V]
           /   \      /
         [A]   [K]  [T]
               /
             [H]
```
B < M → left; A < M, A < B → left of B; K < M, K > B → right of B; H < M, H > B, H < K → left of K; V > M → right; T > M, T < V → left of V.

Each node is stored as **Left pointer | Data | Right pointer**. A pointer holds the **index (address) of the child node**; **−1** (or NULL / 0) means "**no child**". A separate **root pointer** holds the index of the root.

blocks.title: Array representation of the tree 6, 3, 8, 5, 9, 2 (nodes stored in insertion order)

blocks.content: Root pointer = **1**. Node 1 (6) has left → index **2** (3) and right → index **3** (8). Node 2 (3) has left → **6** (2) and right → **4** (5). Leaves have **−1** in both pointers.

// Tree[i].Left, Tree[i].Data, Tree[i].Right; FreePtr = next empty index
PROCEDURE Insert(Value)
    Tree[FreePtr].Data ← Value
    Tree[FreePtr].Left ← -1
    Tree[FreePtr].Right ← -1
    IF Root = -1 THEN
        Root ← FreePtr                       // first node becomes the root
    ELSE
        Current ← Root
        Placed ← FALSE
        WHILE NOT Placed DO
            IF Value < Tree[Current].Data THEN
                IF Tree[Current].Left = -1 THEN
                    Tree[Current].Left ← FreePtr
                    Placed ← TRUE
                ELSE
                    Current ← Tree[Current].Left
                ENDIF
            ELSE
                IF Tree[Current].Right = -1 THEN
                    Tree[Current].Right ← FreePtr
                    Placed ← TRUE
                ELSE
                    Current ← Tree[Current].Right
                ENDIF
            ENDIF
        ENDWHILE
    ENDIF
    FreePtr ← FreePtr + 1
ENDPROCEDURE

blocks.title: Searching for 5 and for 7 in the tree 6, 3, 8, 5, 9, 2
blocks.content:
| Target | Nodes visited | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | 6 (5 < 6, go left) → 3 (5 > 3, go right) → **5** | Found at index 4 after **3** comparisons |
| 7 | 6 (7 > 6, right) → 8 (7 < 8, left) → −1 | **Not found** after 2 comparisons |

Each comparison **discards a whole subtree**, so a **balanced** BST with *n* nodes needs about **log₂ n** comparisons: 1 000 000 nodes → about **20** comparisons, instead of up to 1 000 000 for a linear search.

blocks.title: Unbalanced trees
blocks.content: If values are inserted **already sorted** (1, 2, 3, 4, 5), every node goes to the **right** and the tree becomes a long chain — like a linked list. Searching then takes up to **n** comparisons. A **balanced** tree has roughly equal numbers of nodes in the left and right subtrees.
Visiting **every node exactly once** in a fixed order. The three depth-first traversals differ only in **when the node itself is visited**.

blocks.title: The three traversals
rows: **Copying** a tree (insert in this order to rebuild it)

blocks.content:
PROCEDURE InOrder(Node)
    IF Node <> -1 THEN
        InOrder(Tree[Node].Left)      // 1 left subtree
        OUTPUT Tree[Node].Data        // 2 the node
        InOrder(Tree[Node].Right)     // 3 right subtree
    ENDIF
ENDPROCEDURE

**Q: Complete a binary search tree using 6, 3, 8, 5, 9, 2. Each node is Left pointer | Data | Right pointer. [3]**
Node for **3** points left to **2** and right to **5** (1); **2** is a leaf with −1 pointers (1); **5** is a leaf with −1 pointers (1).

**Q: State the value of the root of the tree built from "M", "B", "A", "K", "H", "V", "T". [1]**
**M** — the first value inserted (1).

**Q: Write the in-order traversal of the tree. [1]**
A, B, H, K, M, T, V (1).

**Q: Explain why a BST may become inefficient. [2]**
If the data is inserted in **sorted order** the tree becomes **unbalanced** — a single chain (1), so a search may visit **every node** instead of about log₂ n (1).

- Putting smaller values on the **right** — smaller go **left**.
- Comparing only with the **root** — keep comparing at each level until an empty position is found.
- Forgetting **−1 / NULL** pointers for leaves.
- Mixing up pre-order (node **first**) and post-order (node **last**).
